Claim: Union of two congruent equilateral triangles cannot be a rectangle.

Proof sketch: Rectangle has 4 right-angle corners. At each corner of rectangle, union must fill 90° wedge. So each rectangle edge must be covered by collinear triangle edge segments. Horizontal rectangle edge: covered by horizontal triangle edges. Each triangle has at most 1 horizontal edge (since its 3 edges are at 3 distinct directions mod 180: 0, 60, 120). If triangle has horizontal edge, then its other edges at 60, 120 (not vertical). Vertical rectangle edge covered by vertical triangle edges: triangle with vertical edge has edges at 90, 30, 150 (not horizontal). So one triangle provides horizontal edges (at most 1), other provides vertical (at most 1). But rectangle needs 2 horizontal edges (top and bottom, disjoint lines) and 2 vertical. Triangle with horizontal edge provides only 1 horizontal line. So top and bottom cannot both be covered. Unless rectangle edge covered by multiple collinear segments from same triangle? Triangle has only 1 edge per direction. So impossible. Also corners: fine. Thus rectangle impossible. Yes.

content:
Looking at each outline:

- **A:** Two triangles (one pointing up, one pointing down) partially overlapping give horizontal top/bottom edges with concave notches on the sides. Possible.
- **B:** Two triangles glued along a full edge form a rhombus. Possible.
- **C:** Two triangles pointing the same direction, offset so one apex lies inside the other, give this arrow-like outline (dashed line is the hidden edge). Possible.
- **D:** Two triangles pointing toward each other, partially overlapping, give vertical side edges with concave notches top and bottom. Possible.
- **E:** A rectangle requires four 90° corners and two pairs of parallel sides (horizontal and vertical). Each equilateral triangle contributes edges in only three directions (mutually at 60°). A triangle supplying horizontal edges cannot supply vertical ones, and vice versa; since each triangle has only one edge per direction, the four sides of a rectangle can never be covered by the edges of just two equilateral triangles. Impossible.

\boxed{E}
